hero.headline: Anthropic files confidentially for initial public offering
hero.body:
Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, has filed confidentially for an initial public offering on the US stock market, the company announced Monday. The confidential filing marks a significant step in the competitive race among AI firms to go public.

The company did not disclose the valuation it will seek on the stock market or provide other terms of the offering. However, Anthropic announced on Thursday that it had raised $65 billion in funding, valuing the company at $965 billion post-money. This represents a substantial increase from its February valuation of $380 billion, making Anthropic the world's most valuable AI startup.

Claude, Anthropic's conversational AI tool, has gained popularity among software engineers and other business clients. The chatbot competes directly with OpenAI's ChatGPT and other AI assistants in both consumer and enterprise markets.

Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI executives and has positioned itself as a leader in AI safety research. The company has raised substantial funding from investors including Google and various venture capital firms.

A confidential filing allows companies to submit their IPO paperwork to securities regulators without immediately making financial information public. This approach gives firms flexibility to assess market conditions and investor interest before committing to a public debut. Anthropic will need to publicly disclose its financial details before shares can begin trading.

The IPO filing comes as multiple major companies prepare to go public. Anthropic's move makes it the first to file ahead of its competitor OpenAI, which is expected to file for a public offering in the coming weeks. Additionally, Elon Musk's SpaceX has filed for a stock market listing at a valuation of approximately $1.75 trillion while seeking $75 billion in investment.

These filings reflect the escalating financial stakes in the AI industry. After years of heavy spending on computing infrastructure and research, AI companies face growing pressure to demonstrate sustainable business models to investors. The path Anthropic takes as a public company could influence how other AI startups decide between remaining private with continued venture backing or pursuing public listings.

The IPO filing represents a significant milestone for the AI sector, which has experienced explosive growth but seen limited exits to public markets. Anthropic did not indicate whether the offering would consist of new shares, sales of existing shareholder stakes, or both. Additional details about the offering are expected to emerge as the process advances.

cards.headline: Iran suspends negotiations with US, threatens to block Strait of Hormuz
cards.body:
Iran and US Navigate Tense Negotiations as Ceasefire Holds

The United States and Iran are navigating a fragile ceasefire that has been tested repeatedly over the past week, with negotiations toward a permanent deal advancing and stalling in unpredictable ways.

The ceasefire, which began on April 7, remains technically in place, though both sides have reported military incidents. On May 4, the US military said it destroyed six Iranian small boats and intercepted Iranian cruise missiles and drones, claims Iran denied. The US also reported that Iran has fired at commercial vessels and seized two container ships since the ceasefire began, though these attacks have so far remained below the threshold that would restart major combat operations.

A major point of contention involves the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway through which roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies pass. Iran has effectively choked off the strait, while the US Navy has been blockading Iranian ports. Trump administration officials announced "Project Freedom" on May 3, a plan to help guide stranded ships through the waterway. However, Iranian officials warned that any American intervention in managing the strait would violate the ceasefire. After beginning the operation on May 4, Trump paused Project Freedom just one day later, announcing the pause would give space for peace negotiations.

According to reporting from May 6, Washington and Tehran were close to agreeing on a one-page memorandum of understanding. Trump said he expected Iran to respond to several key points within 48 hours. However, recent reporting indicates Trump is seeking edits to the proposed agreement, with requested changes related to the Strait of Hormuz and the removal of highly enriched uranium.

Trump has sent mixed signals about his commitment to a deal. On May 5, Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared "the operation is over" and said the US was focused on negotiations. But Trump has also threatened escalation, writing on social media that if Iran does not agree to the terms, "the bombing starts, and it will be, sadly, at a much higher level and intensity than it was before."

The negotiations have been complicated by broader regional tensions and Trump's own statements. In public remarks, Trump described a recent US operation to seize an Iranian ship as acting "like pirates," noting the US took the ship's cargo and oil. He also made threats that Iranian forces would be "blown off the face of the earth" if they attacked US vessels.

Oil prices have fluctuated with each development, trading between roughly $109 and $114 per barrel as markets react to the unpredictable course of negotiations. Officials in Pakistan, who have been helping facilitate talks, described negotiations as remaining "difficult," even as both sides have indicated they are seeking a resolution to avoid further escalation.

cards.headline: Israel Orders Strikes on Beirut Suburbs as Hezbollah Conflict Escalates
cards.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered military strikes on the southern suburbs of Beirut following intensified attacks from the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah. The operation marks a significant expansion of the conflict, bringing direct military action to Lebanon's capital for the first time in this round of fighting.

The escalation came after Hezbollah launched what it called "Operation Chewed Wheat," coordinated with Iranian forces. The group fired more than 200 rockets toward Israeli territory, including at military bases in Haifa, Tel Aviv, and Beersheba. Most projectiles were intercepted or fell in open areas, though two people were injured. Israel responded with intense bombardment of Beirut's southern suburbs and southern Lebanon throughout Thursday.

Israel issued sweeping evacuation orders covering a zone extending 25 miles from the Lebanese border, instructing residents north of the Zahrani River to leave immediately. The orders affect major cities including Nabatieh and dozens of villages. An additional evacuation order was issued for a neighborhood in central Beirut near restaurants, where Israel said it would strike a building.

Nearly a million people have been internally displaced over 10 days of fighting. Residents expressed desperation over the orders. Hamza Zbeeb, a municipal official from Nimiriya, asked: "Where can I go? Many people have gone to Beirut and returned because there's nowhere to stay. I don't want to be on the streets."

Israeli warplanes struck two buildings in central Beirut's Zouq Blat neighborhood, leveling them after warning residents to evacuate. One building was next to a shelter housing displaced families, creating large crowds in the main square seeking refuge. The other struck near the prime minister's office, UN agencies, and foreign embassies.

The Lebanese health ministry reported 70 people killed in Thursday's strikes. Among the dead were two academics, Hussein Bazzi and Murtadha Sarour, killed in an attack on Lebanese University's campus. Lebanon's president, Joseph Aoun, condemned the strike as a "flagrant violation of international laws and norms."

Israel's military stated it was targeting Hezbollah's missile launchers and warned of an imminent campaign of "overwhelming force." A spokesperson said residents should distance themselves from affected areas immediately.

Human rights organizations described the evacuation orders as forced displacement that could amount to war crimes. They argued that Israeli forces should still work to prevent civilian harm even if residents do not evacuate.

The exchange represented the most severe escalation yet in the 10-day conflict, with Hezbollah and Iran coordinating attacks for the first time. Israeli strikes have killed at least 634 people and injured 1,586 across Lebanon.

cards.headline: Oil prices climb after U.S. and Iran military strikes
cards.teaser: Oil prices rose as investors assessed renewed military confrontations between the United States and Iran while both nations continue negotiations.
cards.body:
Oil prices climbed following military exchanges between the United States and Iran. The U.S. military bombed Iranian radar and drone control sites after Tehran shot down an American MQ-1 Predator drone. American aircraft struck several Iranian locations, including Qeeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait also reported that its air defenses opened fire on Monday.

Investors reacted to the escalation by reassessing risks to global energy supplies. The market concerns centered on potential disruptions to oil production and shipping routes in the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz region.

cards.headline: Multiple people killed in Oregon shooting, officer wounded
cards.teaser: A domestic violence incident in Sandy, Oregon left multiple people dead and a police officer shot.
cards.body:
Multiple people were killed and a police officer was wounded in Sandy, Oregon following a domestic violence incident. The suspected shooter has been identified and faces multiple murder and kidnapping charges, according to local authorities.

Police described the incident as traumatic and said it began as a domestic disturbance. The officer who was shot sustained injuries during the response. Authorities have not released the names of the victims or additional details about the circumstances of the shooting.

cards.headline: Trump administration closes AI chip export loophole
cards.teaser: Commerce Department clarifies that advanced AI chips cannot be sold to firms with Chinese parent companies regardless of location.
cards.body:
The Trump administration moved to close a potential loophole in U.S. export restrictions on Sunday, clarifying that companies need a license to sell advanced AI chips to firms with Chinese parent companies even if those firms are not located in China or another restricted country. The Commerce Department issued new guidance addressing the 2023 licensing requirements.

The clarification targets a gap that could have allowed Chinese-owned companies operating outside China to acquire advanced AI chips without the restrictions that apply to entities in China. The 2023 export controls were designed to prevent China from accessing cutting-edge semiconductor technology that could be used for military applications or to advance Chinese AI capabilities.

cards.headline: Federal Reserve officials warn AI costs may outpace benefits
cards.teaser: Several Fed officials say AI-related investment is boosting demand faster than productivity gains materialize.
cards.body:
Several Federal Reserve officials have cautioned that artificial intelligence's economic costs may materialize faster than its promised gains, challenging the assumption that AI will help solve inflation problems. The officials point to stronger evidence of AI-driven investment increasing demand for workers and equipment than evidence of productivity improvements materializing.

These warnings take on particular significance as the Fed operates under new leadership from Kevin Warsh, who has argued that AI's supply-side advantages justify maintaining lower interest rates. The question of how AI will influence inflation and productivity has become central to shaping monetary policy decisions. Some Fed officials now contend that the technology's impact on demand could complicate the effort to control prices before any productivity benefits actually emerge.

The debate reflects a broader tension within the Federal Reserve about how to interpret AI's economic impact. While technology enthusiasts and some policymakers expect AI to boost supply-side capacity and help reduce inflation over time, several Fed officials worry that demand effects are arriving first. Businesses appear to be spending heavily on AI infrastructure and hiring workers to implement new systems, which adds to inflationary pressures in the near term.

This concern carries weight given the Fed's historical focus on managing inflation expectations. If demand surges outpace productivity gains, the central bank may face pressure to maintain higher interest rates for longer than some officials prefer. This creates a dilemma for Warsh and other officials who believe lower rates are justified by AI's long-term potential.

The productivity question remains unresolved. While companies have invested billions in AI capabilities, widespread evidence of actual productivity improvements across the economy has not yet materialized at scale. This timing gap between investment and results means the Fed must make policy decisions based partly on expectations about future productivity rather than current data.

Fed officials highlighting the demand-side risks appear concerned that policymakers and markets may be getting ahead of themselves in assuming AI will quickly solve persistent inflation challenges. Inflation has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target despite months of interest rate increases, suggesting that supply-side solutions may not arrive as quickly as some have hoped.

The debate matters because it affects decisions on interest rates, which ripple through the broader economy and influence borrowing costs for businesses and consumers. If demand effects dominate in the near term, the Fed may need to keep rates higher to prevent inflation from accelerating further. If productivity improvements arrive sooner than skeptics expect, lower rates could eventually prove justified.

As the Fed charts its course, officials will need to balance optimism about AI's long-term potential against wariness about its immediate economic effects. The outcome of this debate will significantly influence monetary policy direction and broader economic outcomes in coming months.

cards.headline: Ethiopia Holds Election Amid Fears of Renewed Tigray Conflict
cards.teaser: Voting has been suspended in parts of Ethiopia over security concerns as Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's party is expected to dominate.
cards.body:
Ethiopia held national elections as security concerns forced voting to be suspended in some areas. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's party is expected to secure a dominant position in the results.

The election takes place against a backdrop of significant challenges for the nation. Ethiopia faces the prospect of renewed conflict in the Tigray region and ongoing tensions with neighboring Eritrea over Red Sea access, issues that loom large over the electoral process and the country's political trajectory.

cards.headline: Two Syrian Officers Face War Crime Charges in Austria
cards.teaser: Austria's first trial against Assad regime officials gives Syrian witnesses a chance to confront two men accused of torture.
cards.body:
Two Syrian officers who lived undetected are now facing war crime charges in Austria. The trial marks the first time Austrian courts have prosecuted officials from the Assad regime for alleged atrocities committed during Syria's civil war.

The proceedings will provide a rare opportunity for Syrian witnesses to directly confront the two men they have accused of torture. The officers had been hiding in plain sight before their identities and alleged roles in war crimes were discovered.

cards.headline: Alberta to Vote on Whether to Hold Referendum on Leaving Canada
cards.teaser: Albertans will decide in October if they want to stay in Canada or hold a referendum on separation.
cards.body:
Alberta's movement to separate from Canada will face a decisive vote in October. Residents of the western Canadian province will be asked whether they want to remain part of Canada or proceed with holding a referendum on leaving the country.

The vote represents a significant moment for the long-running separatist movement in Alberta. The outcome could either settle the question of Alberta's place in Canada or deepen existing divisions between the province and the federal government.

cards.headline: Britain Denies Entry to Social Media Personalities Cenk Uygur and Hasan Piker
cards.teaser: British authorities barred two popular social media figures, saying their presence may not be conducive to the public good.
cards.body:
British authorities have denied entry to US citizens Cenk Uygur and Hasan Piker, left-wing content creators with large online followings. The pair were scheduled to speak at the SXSW London festival and at Oxford this week.

The Home Office said their presence "may not be conducive to the public good" but provided no explanation for the decision. Both men have substantial audiences on social media where they discuss political and social issues.

cards.headline: UK Releases Files on Peter Mandelson's Ties to Jeffrey Epstein
cards.teaser: More than a thousand pages of documents reveal new information about the ex-diplomat who was fired over his links to Epstein.
cards.body:
Britain released more than a thousand pages of documents about Peter Mandelson, a former diplomat who was fired over his links to Jeffrey Epstein. The files include a letter from Mandelson making claims that were not previously public.

The document release adds to growing scrutiny of Mandelson, who has faced questions about his connections to various senior figures. The files bring additional concerns for Prime Minister Keir Starmer as his government deals with the fallout from the revelations.

cards.headline: Singer Dua Lipa Marries Actor Callum Turner in London
cards.teaser: The wedding took place at Old Marylebone Town Hall, a venue that has hosted ceremonies for multiple celebrities.
cards.body:
Dua Lipa and Callum Turner were married at Old Marylebone Town Hall in London. The venue is among the busiest wedding locations in Britain and has a history of hosting high-profile ceremonies.

Old Marylebone Town Hall has been the site of weddings for celebrities including Sylvester Stallone, Paul McCartney, and Lena Dunham. The historic venue continues to be a popular choice for public figures seeking to marry in the British capital.

cards.headline: Colorado governor commutes sentence of former county clerk Tina Peters
cards.teaser: Tina Peters, a former county clerk convicted for election-related crimes, was released from prison after Governor Jared Polis commuted her sentence.
cards.body:
Former Mesa County clerk Tina Peters was released from prison after Colorado Governor Jared Polis commuted her sentence. Peters, who promoted election conspiracy theories linked to the 2020 election, had served less than a quarter of her nine-year sentence before her release.

According to the Colorado corrections department, Peters was discharged on Monday. The 70-year-old had been convicted of participating in a scheme to advance election conspiracy theories. Her release has divided communities across Colorado.

cards.headline: AI company Anthropic plans to go public on US stock market
cards.teaser: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, announced plans to offer shares to the public later this year.
cards.body:
Anthropic has filed confidentially for an initial public offering on the US stock market, marking a major milestone in the AI industry's race to go public. The company, which developed the Claude chatbot, announced the filing on Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The startup's valuation has surged dramatically, reaching $965 billion following a recent $65 billion funding round. This represents a significant jump from its $380 billion valuation in February, reflecting growing investor confidence in the AI sector and Anthropic's position as a leading competitor in the market.

cards.headline: Iowa Democrat tests strategy of attacking Senate Majority Leader Schumer
cards.teaser: A Democratic candidate in Iowa is running a campaign that includes criticizing Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, testing whether distancing from party leadership can succeed in a red state.
cards.body:
Rob Sand, Iowa's most prominent Democrat, is running for governor while positioning himself as a critic of the two-party political system. The candidate, known for discussing his love of hunting and opening rallies with America the Beautiful, distinguishes himself from national Democratic leadership.

Democrats view Sand's candidacy as a potential breakthrough in a state that has shifted solidly Republican. Party officials believe his unconventional approach and appeal to rural voters could help Democrats win key offices in the November midterm elections.

cards.headline: Two US commentators denied entry to United Kingdom
cards.teaser: Left-wing content creators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur were blocked from entering the UK by the Home Office.
cards.body:
The British Home Office has prevented US commentators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur from entering the country. The two were scheduled to speak at the SXSW London festival and Oxford University this week.

Both men are left-wing content creators with substantial online audiences. The Home Office has not publicly disclosed its reasons for the denial.

cards.headline: London Underground strikes set to proceed after negotiations fail
cards.teaser: Members of the RMT union will strike on the London Tube this week following unsuccessful talks over working hours.
cards.body:
London Underground workers represented by the RMT union will strike on Tuesday and Thursday this week after negotiations with management failed to reach agreement on working hours. The union members voted to proceed with the action once talks broke down.

The strikes will cause significant disruption to millions of commuters who depend on the Tube network for their daily travel.

cards.headline: Barry Diller's company prepares takeover offer for MGM Resorts
cards.teaser: People Inc. is preparing a bid to acquire the remaining portion of MGM Resorts it does not already own, valuing the casino company at $18 billion.
cards.body:
Media mogul Barry Diller's People Inc. has proposed acquiring MGM Resorts International at a valuation exceeding $18 billion. The bid would give People Inc. full ownership of the casino operator, consolidating the company's existing stake into complete control.

The move represents a significant strategic shift for Diller's digital media company. Just weeks before the takeover proposal, Diller told shareholders that People would intensify its focus on MGM, describing the casino operator's stock as "wildly undervalued."

cards.headline: Florida sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over AI safety
cards.teaser: Florida's attorney general filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging the company prioritized profits over safety concerns.
cards.body:
Florida's attorney general has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging the company prioritizes profits over safety concerns. The lawsuit claims OpenAI has failed to adequately address risks posed by its AI systems, including ChatGPT, which millions of people use.

The legal action centers on accusations that OpenAI has not implemented sufficient safeguards to prevent misuse or harmful outputs from its AI models. The state argues the company has neglected necessary steps to protect against potential harms from its widely deployed technology.

cards.headline: Wise under investigation for money laundering controls
cards.teaser: The money transfer company Wise disclosed it is cooperating with an investigation by the Brussels prosecutor's office into its anti-money laundering procedures.
cards.body:
Wise, the international money transfer service, is under investigation by the Brussels prosecutor's office over its money laundering controls. The company is cooperating with authorities on the matter.

Wise stated it has not received any specific findings from the investigation to date. The probe examines whether the firm has adequate systems to detect and prevent illicit financial activity on its platform.

cards.headline: United Airlines flight returns after Bluetooth device naming incident
cards.teaser: A United Airlines flight bound for Spain turned back to Newark after a passenger named a Bluetooth device using threatening language.
cards.body:
A United Airlines flight departing Newark for Spain turned back to the airport after a passenger's Bluetooth device displayed an offensive name that raised security concerns. The device's name prompted the flight crew to return to Newark, where passengers underwent additional screening.

The incident caused significant delays to the transatlantic service as authorities addressed the situation. Once resolved, passengers were cleared to continue their journey.

cards.headline: Remote work linked to weaker hiring of young workers
cards.teaser: A Federal Reserve study found that remote work, rather than artificial intelligence, may be contributing to employment challenges for younger college graduates.
cards.body:
Research from the New York Federal Reserve suggests that the shift to remote work has made it harder for young workers to find jobs. The study challenges the common assumption that artificial intelligence is the primary factor behind weak entry-level hiring.

Younger college graduates appear to face particular disadvantages in a remote work environment, where they may have fewer opportunities to learn from experienced colleagues and build professional networks. The findings indicate that changes in workplace structure, rather than automation, are creating barriers to employment for people early in their careers.

cards.headline: Wall Street near record highs as tech gains offset Iran tensions
cards.teaser: Stock markets hovered near record levels as gains in technology companies, including Nvidia, balanced investor concerns about escalating conflict with Iran
cards.body:
U.S. and Iranian forces exchanged military strikes around the Strait of Hormuz, with Kuwait condemning repeated Iranian attacks. Despite the escalating tensions, oil prices climbed only moderately as investors assessed that both nations remained engaged in negotiations.

Wall Street hovered near record highs, with technology stocks like Nvidia leading gains that outweighed concerns about the regional conflict. The market's resilience reflected investor confidence that the geopolitical tensions would not derail economic growth or tech sector momentum.

cards.headline: Nvidia introduces RTX Spark chips for AI-focused Windows computers
cards.teaser: The new chips combine Arm processors with RTX graphics and unified memory for laptop workstations and desktop PCs.
cards.body:
Nvidia has launched RTX Spark, a new superchip designed to bring advanced AI capabilities directly to laptops and desktop computers. The chip combines Arm-based processors with RTX graphics processing units and unified memory architecture. The company says the technology could fundamentally change how people interact with computers, potentially replacing traditional mouse and keyboard input with AI agents.

ASUS and Microsoft have already announced devices powered by the new chips, including the ASUS ProArt P16 and P14 laptops alongside a mini PC. Nvidia also introduced a DGX Station for Windows, bringing trillion-parameter AI capabilities to enterprise desktops. The move puts Nvidia in direct competition with Intel, Apple, Qualcomm and AMD in the race to dominate AI computing on personal devices.

cards.headline: SpaceX warns potential investors of possible major stock dilution
cards.teaser: The space company added a disclosure that significant equity could be issued in future transactions after it goes public.
cards.body:
SpaceX has warned prospective investors that major dilution of their stakes could occur after the company completes its initial public offering. The disclosure appeared in updated materials provided to potential investors.

The warning indicates SpaceX may issue substantial amounts of new equity in future transactions. Such dilution would reduce the ownership percentage of existing shareholders. The company has not yet set a date for its public debut or disclosed how much equity might be issued.

cards.headline: Weather forecasting startup beats government predictions by days
cards.teaser: Windborne Systems released a weather model that outperforms the best government forecasts.
cards.body:
Windborne Systems has developed a weather forecasting model that surpasses predictions from government agencies. The AI-based system produces more accurate forecasts with longer lead times than traditional models.

The company claims its newest model beats the most advanced government weather predictions by multiple days. This performance advantage could have implications for industries that depend on weather forecasting, including agriculture, aviation, and emergency management. Windborne Systems operates as a private startup focused on atmospheric modeling.

cards.headline: Former Meta technology chief raises $250 million climate fund
cards.teaser: Mike Schroepfer's Gigascale Capital will back companies building solutions for energy and material shortages.
cards.body:
Mike Schroepfer, Meta's former chief technology officer, has launched Gigascale Capital with $250 million in funding. The investment firm will back founders developing climate-friendly technologies to address global energy and material shortages.

The fund represents a contrarian approach in venture capital, which has recently concentrated on artificial intelligence and software investments. Schroepfer is now focused on supporting climate technology solutions across multiple sectors.

cards.headline: DuckDuckGo launches browser extensions to simplify access to AI-free search
cards.teaser: The privacy-focused search engine released extensions for Chrome and Firefox as its traffic grows.
cards.body:
DuckDuckGo has released browser extensions for Chrome and Firefox that make it easier to access its search engine without AI-generated results. The extensions enable users to quickly switch to the company's traditional web search, avoiding artificial intelligence summaries and features.

The move reflects DuckDuckGo's positioning as an alternative to mainstream search engines that have increasingly integrated AI into their results. The company has reported growing traffic to its service, and the extensions are now available through the respective browser stores.

cards.headline: Revolut begins rolling out banking services to users in India
cards.teaser: The British fintech company is preparing for a broader launch after building a waitlist of 450,000 users.
cards.body:
Revolut has started rolling out banking services to thousands of users in India as it prepares for a broader market launch. The British fintech company has built a waitlist of approximately 450,000 people in the country, indicating significant demand for its services.

The gradual rollout allows Revolut to test its operations in India's market before expanding access more widely. The company offers digital banking services including accounts, payments, and currency exchange to users across multiple countries globally.

hero.headline: Kevin Keegan reveals stage four cancer diagnosis
hero.body:
Kevin Keegan, the former England manager and Newcastle United icon, has publicly revealed he has stage four cancer. The 75-year-old initially had his diagnosis announced by his family in January, but provided an update on his condition during a recent appearance at the Tyne Theatre and Opera House.

"They said we have a top doctor with this new way of fighting what you have got, which is stage four cancer," Keegan said in remarks reported by the Daily Mail. "He was a Liverpool supporter so I went to meet him. I knew I wouldn't be walking alone, if you know what I mean."

Keegan had been admitted to hospital for evaluation of ongoing abdominal symptoms before tests confirmed his diagnosis. His family released a statement expressing gratitude to the medical team involved in his care and requesting privacy during this difficult period.

Keegan's playing career stands as one of English football's most distinguished. He earned 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals for his country and captaining the side 31 times. He competed in the 1982 World Cup and won two Ballon d'Or awards as European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979.

As a club player, Keegan achieved remarkable success. He helped Liverpool win three English league titles while also securing the European Cup, two UEFA Cups, and the FA Cup. He later won the Bundesliga with Hamburg, cementing his status as one of Europe's finest footballers during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

His managerial career proved equally memorable. Keegan took charge of Newcastle United in 1992, overseeing the club's promotion to the top flight before building what became known as "The Entertainers". His Newcastle side topped the Premier League table for much of the 1995-96 season but ultimately finished as runners-up to Manchester United in a dramatic title race.

After leaving Newcastle in 1997, Keegan managed Fulham before becoming England manager from 1999 until his resignation in 2000. He then spent four years at Manchester City before returning to Newcastle for a brief eight-month spell in 2008 that ended amid boardroom tensions with owner Mike Ashley and director of football Dennis Wise. Following his departure from Newcastle, Keegan successfully pursued a constructive dismissal case and was awarded 2 million pounds in damages by an independent Premier League tribunal in 2009.

Newcastle United has sent their heartfelt support and warmest wishes to Keegan during his treatment. The club and football community have rallied behind the former manager as he faces this serious health challenge.

cards.headline: Raymond Berry, Hall of Fame receiver and coach, dies at 93
cards.teaser: Raymond Berry, the Pro Football Hall of Fame receiver who won two NFL championships with the Baltimore Colts, has died at age 93.
cards.body:
Berry played 13 seasons in the NFL and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame for his accomplishments as a receiver with the Baltimore Colts. He won two NFL championships during his playing career with the team.

After his playing days ended, Berry transitioned to coaching and later won a Super Bowl as head coach of the New England Patriots. His career spanned both sides of the game, leaving a mark on professional football as both a player and coach over several decades.

cards.headline: Serena Williams to return to tennis at age 44
cards.teaser: Serena Williams will return to competitive tennis after nearly four years away from the sport, playing doubles at Queen's Club.
cards.body:
Williams, 44, is making her competitive return to tennis at Queen's Club after nearly four years away from the sport. She last competed at the 2022 US Open. Williams will play in the women's doubles draw at the WTA 500 event, partnering with Victoria Mboko.

Williams described Queen's as the "perfect place" for her comeback. She has called her departure from tennis an "evolving away" rather than a retirement, though she remained on the retired players' list until recently.

cards.headline: Knicks and Spurs set for NBA Finals matchup
cards.teaser: The New York Knicks will face the San Antonio Spurs in the 2026 NBA Finals, with ABC's coverage beginning June 3.
cards.body:
The NBA Finals will feature the New York Knicks against the San Antonio Spurs, a matchup that seemed unlikely before the playoffs began. The series will showcase Spurs center Victor Wembanyama against the Knicks roster in what analysts view as a defining series for both franchises.

ABC will provide exclusive coverage of the Finals starting June 3. The matchup presents storylines around the young Spurs star and the Knicks' return to championship contention, with both teams defying preseason expectations to reach the finals.

cards.headline: French Open fines player $76,000 for sexist remark about umpire
cards.teaser: Adolfo Daniel Vallejo of Paraguay has been fined $76,000 by French Open organizers after making a sexist comment about a female chair umpire.
cards.body:
Adolfo Daniel Vallejo has been fined $65,000-$76,000 by Roland Garros officials for making sexist comments about a female umpire following his exit from the tournament. Organizers deemed the remarks "clearly unacceptable."

The penalty ranks among the largest conduct fines issued at the French Open, underscoring the tournament's commitment to enforcing professional standards among competitors.

cards.headline: WhatsApp messages reveal Southampton spying campaign
cards.teaser: New WhatsApp messages show Southampton orchestrated a spying operation against Championship rivals, with club management approving the efforts.
cards.body:
Messages obtained from Southampton officials reveal the club conducted surveillance operations targeting rival Championship teams. One message included praise for the effort, with text reading "You legend. Manager loved it," indicating the manager was aware of and supported the spying activities.

The revelation adds Southampton to a list of clubs involved in spying scandals in English football. The messages provide direct evidence of how the campaign was organized and approved at multiple levels within the club's hierarchy.

cards.headline: Chicago Bears stadium deal stalls in Illinois legislature
cards.teaser: The Illinois legislature adjourned without passing a stadium bill for the Chicago Bears, leaving open the possibility of a move to Indiana.
cards.body:
A proposed bill that would have helped keep the Bears in Illinois failed to pass before the state legislature adjourned for the summer. The measure was not included in the $55 billion state budget that did pass, leaving the team's long-term location uncertain.

The Bears released a statement following the legislature's adjournment. The team has explored options for a new stadium, including potential sites in both Illinois and Indiana. The legislative failure means stadium negotiations remain unresolved heading into the summer recess.

hero.headline: Florida Sues OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman Over User Safety Claims
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed an 83-page lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman in Florida circuit court, accusing the company of prioritizing profits over user safety. The complaint alleges that Altman led a company built on what the state describes as a web of deceit and exploitation of users, including Florida residents.

The lawsuit claims Altman showed utter disregard for the risk to human life in his leadership of the artificial intelligence company. OpenAI has emerged as one of the most prominent AI companies in recent years, with its ChatGPT product gaining widespread adoption among consumers and businesses. The Florida legal action represents one of the most significant state-level challenges to the AI industry's rapid expansion.

The complaint focuses on allegations that OpenAI exploited its users while building its business. Florida's case adds to growing scrutiny of AI companies and their practices as lawmakers and regulators work to understand the technology's risks and benefits. The state's legal action comes as questions mount about how AI companies handle user data, protect privacy, and ensure their products do not cause harm.

The lawsuit marks an aggressive stance by Florida officials against a major technology company. Uthmeier's office filed the action as part of what appears to be a broader effort to hold tech companies accountable for their practices. The case could set precedents for how states regulate AI companies and what responsibilities those companies bear for user protection.

OpenAI has not publicly responded to the lawsuit. The legal battle comes at a time when the company continues to expand its operations and release new products. The outcome of Florida's case could influence how other states approach regulation of AI companies and whether additional legal challenges follow.

The case will test questions about corporate responsibility in the AI sector and what standards companies must meet when deploying powerful technologies that affect millions of users. This lawsuit comes amid a period of heightened legal and regulatory attention to major technology companies. Recent court actions have targeted major tech firms over various practices, from data handling to content moderation decisions.

The timing of Florida's action reflects broader concerns within state governments about the rapid deployment of AI systems without sufficient safety measures or oversight. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into daily life for millions of Americans, regulators are moving to establish clearer standards and hold companies accountable for potential harms.

The case could establish important legal precedent for how states can hold AI companies responsible for user protection. If successful, the lawsuit might encourage other states to pursue similar actions against technology companies, creating a patchwork of state-level AI regulation that could shape how companies operate across the country.

cards.headline: James Gunn Reveals Lex Luthor Warsuit for Superman Sequel
cards.teaser: Director James Gunn shared a first look at Nicholas Hoult wearing Lex Luthor's warsuit during production of Man of Tomorrow.
cards.body:
Director James Gunn revealed a first look at the warsuit for Lex Luthor in the upcoming Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow. The image shows actor Nicholas Hoult wearing the villain's iconic armor as production continues on the film. Gunn posted the reveal with the caption "Fit check. Live from the set of Man of Tomorrow."

Hoult plays Lex Luthor in the sequel to Gunn's Superman film. The warsuit represents one of the character's most recognizable elements from comic book storylines, giving the villain enhanced strength and weaponry to combat Superman. Production on Man of Tomorrow is currently underway with Gunn directing.

cards.headline: Ariana Grande Stars With Justin Long in New Music Video
cards.teaser: The singer released a horror-inspired video for "Hate That I Made You Love Me" featuring actor Justin Long.
cards.body:
Ariana Grande released a new music video for her single "Hate That I Made You Love Me" featuring actor Justin Long in a darkly comedic horror story. Christian Breslauer directed the video, which follows Long as the supposedly dead-and-buried singer haunts him everywhere he goes. Janusz Kaminski, cinematographer known for his work on Steven Spielberg films, shot the video.

Breslauer previously directed Grande's short film "Brighter Days Ahead" from her 2024 album Eternal Sunshine. The new video marks another collaboration between the director and singer. The single is Grande's latest release following her previous album work.

cards.headline: Variety Launches Power of Women Event in London
cards.teaser: Publisher Dea Lawrence announced the expansion of the Power of Women franchise to the UK capital.
cards.body:
Variety publisher and co-president Dea Lawrence unveiled the Power of Women franchise in London, marking the publication's expansion of this major event to the UK market. Lawrence told attendees it is an opportune moment for British talent in entertainment.

The launch reflects the current strength of British creative talent and production capabilities. Power of Women is one of Variety's flagship franchises, and bringing it to London underscores the vitality of the UK entertainment sector.

cards.headline: Tim Curry Returns for Stream 2: Sudden Death
cards.teaser: The actor will reprise his role in an expanded capacity for the horror sequel.
cards.body:
Tim Curry will return in an expanded role in Stream 2: Sudden Death. Fuzz on the Lens Productions, the team behind Terrifier 2, Terrifier 3 and Screamboat, is producing the sequel. Brian Q Quinn of Impractical Jokers wrote the screenplay with longtime Impractical Jokers producer Joe Imburgio.

Michael Leavy oversaw the project for the production company. The original Stream featured Curry in a smaller capacity. The sequel represents a continuation of the horror franchise with an increased role for the veteran actor.

cards.headline: Billy Strings Performs With Les Claypool at Detroit Show
cards.teaser: The bluegrass musician played his first show since breaking his leg in a skateboarding accident.
cards.body:
Bluegrass musician Billy Strings made his return to performing at a Detroit concert with Primus bassist Les Claypool, his friend and fishing buddy. Strings sat on a stool during the performance as he recovered from a skateboarding accident that left him with a broken leg.

The collaboration brought together artists from different musical worlds, with Strings joining Claypool for the show. The seated setup allowed the bluegrass musician to perform while continuing his injury recovery.

cards.headline: Katey Sagal Joins Elizabeth Banks Apple TV Comedy
cards.teaser: The actress will appear in the untitled series from Liz Heldens and Matt Ward.
cards.body: Katey Sagal joined the cast of an untitled Apple TV comedy from Liz Heldens and Matt Ward. She will appear alongside lead Elizabeth Banks and cast members Ted Danson and Rob De

hero.headline: Federal Reserve officials warn AI costs may outpace benefits
hero.teaser: Several Fed officials say AI-related investment is boosting demand faster than productivity gains materialize.
hero.body:
Several Federal Reserve officials have cautioned that artificial intelligence's economic costs may materialize faster than its promised gains, challenging the assumption that AI will help solve inflation problems. The officials point to stronger evidence of AI-driven investment increasing demand for workers and equipment than evidence of productivity improvements materializing.

These warnings take on particular significance as the Fed operates under new leadership from Kevin Warsh, who has argued that AI's supply-side advantages justify maintaining lower interest rates. The question of how AI will influence inflation and productivity has become central to shaping monetary policy decisions. Some Fed officials now contend that the technology's impact on demand could complicate the effort to control prices before any productivity benefits actually emerge.

The debate reflects a broader tension within the Federal Reserve about how to interpret AI's economic impact. While technology enthusiasts and some policymakers expect AI to boost supply-side capacity and help reduce inflation over time, several Fed officials worry that demand effects are arriving first. Businesses appear to be spending heavily on AI infrastructure and hiring workers to implement new systems, which adds to inflationary pressures in the near term.

This concern carries weight given the Fed's historical focus on managing inflation expectations. If demand surges outpace productivity gains, the central bank may face pressure to maintain higher interest rates for longer than some officials prefer. This creates a dilemma for Warsh and other officials who believe lower rates are justified by AI's long-term potential.

The productivity question remains unresolved. While companies have invested billions in AI capabilities, widespread evidence of actual productivity improvements across the economy has not yet materialized at scale. This timing gap between investment and results means the Fed must make policy decisions based partly on expectations about future productivity rather than current data.

Fed officials highlighting the demand-side risks appear concerned that policymakers and markets may be getting ahead of themselves in assuming AI will quickly solve persistent inflation challenges. Inflation has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target despite months of interest rate increases, suggesting that supply-side solutions may not arrive as quickly as some have hoped.

The debate matters because it affects decisions on interest rates, which ripple through the broader economy and influence borrowing costs for businesses and consumers. If demand effects dominate in the near term, the Fed may need to keep rates higher to prevent inflation from accelerating further. If productivity improvements arrive sooner than skeptics expect, lower rates could eventually prove justified.

As the Fed charts its course, officials will need to balance optimism about AI's long-term potential against wariness about its immediate economic effects. The outcome of this debate will significantly influence monetary policy direction and broader economic outcomes in coming months.

cards.headline: Trump administration closes AI chip export loophole
cards.teaser: Commerce Department clarifies that advanced AI chips cannot be sold to firms with Chinese parent companies regardless of location.
cards.body:
The Trump administration moved to close a potential loophole in U.S. export restrictions on Sunday, clarifying that companies need a license to sell advanced AI chips to firms with Chinese parent companies even if those firms are not located in China or another restricted country. The Commerce Department issued new guidance addressing the 2023 licensing requirements.

The clarification targets a gap that could have allowed Chinese-owned companies operating outside China to acquire advanced AI chips without the restrictions that apply to entities in China. The 2023 export controls were designed to prevent China from accessing cutting-edge semiconductor technology that could be used for military applications or to advance Chinese AI capabilities.

cards.headline: US military kills three in fourth drug boat strike in a week
cards.teaser: The U.S.
cards.body:
The U.S. military conducted another strike on a boat suspected of smuggling drugs in the eastern Pacific Ocean over the weekend, killing three men aboard. This marks the fourth such attack carried out within a week.

The strikes have resulted in a combined death toll of 205, according to U.S. military statements. The eastern Pacific remains a major transit route for narcotics headed toward the United States from South American production zones.

cards.headline: Jill Biden defends Hunter Biden pardon
cards.teaser: The former first lady said the family believed Trump would target Hunter Biden after the election.
cards.body:
Former first lady Jill Biden defended the pardon issued to her stepson Hunter Biden by former President Biden in a recent interview. She explained that the family's decision changed after Trump's election victory, saying they knew Trump would target Hunter Biden.

The pardon, issued before President Biden left office, covered federal charges against his son. The decision sparked criticism from both political parties when it was announced.

cards.headline: New York mayor skips Israel Day parade
cards.teaser: Zohran Mamdani announced days in advance he would not attend the annual Fifth Avenue event.
cards.body:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani did not attend the city's annual Israel Day parade on Sunday, breaking with political tradition. The parade took place along Fifth Avenue as it does each year.

Mamdani announced his decision days in advance at a press conference on Thursday, telling New Yorkers he would not appear at the event. The absence marks a departure from how previous New York mayors have handled the parade, which has been a fixture on the city's political calendar.

cards.headline: Pro-Trump candidate leads Colombian presidential race
cards.teaser: Aberaldo de la Espriella captured 43.74 percent in the first round and heads to a runoff.
cards.body:
Right-wing outsider Abelardo de la Espriella won the first round of Colombia's presidential election, securing a spot in the June 21 runoff. Known for his tough-on-crime stance, de la Espriella has positioned himself as an ally of President Trump and appealed to voters seeking a new conservative direction.

He will face left-wing senator Iván Cepeda, who is allied with outgoing President Gustavo Petro, in the final ballot. De la Espriella's first-round victory demonstrates voter appetite for the political outsider's conservative platform.

cards.headline: House Speaker Johnson meets with Trump
cards.teaser: The meeting took place as Congress prepares for upcoming legislative sessions.
cards.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson met with President Trump, according to reports. The meeting comes as Congress faces a busy legislative calendar in the coming months.

No details about the topics discussed or outcomes of the meeting were released. Johnson has worked to maintain his relationship with Trump while managing a narrow Republican majority in the House of Representatives.
